definitions.definition: The 'vajra vehicle': the esoteric Mahāyāna that attains buddhahood swiftly by mantra, consecration, deity yoga and the yogas of the subtle body, with the vajra (indestructible emptiness and gnosis) as its emblem.
The 'way of mantra' within the Mahāyāna, contrasted with the way of the perfections: the same goal reached by more means, without confusion, without hardship, for the sharp-witted.
The way of the perfections (the sūtra Mahāyāna), the 'causal vehicle' that reaches buddhahood over countless aeons; in tantric doxography the lower of the two Mahāyāna ways.

cross_language.form: pha rol tu phyin pa'i tshul

definitions.definition: A text revealed by the Buddha (as Vajradhara) teaching mantra, maṇḍala, consecration and yoga; explained as 'continuum' (prabandha) — of ground, path and fruit (cause, method and result).

notes: The 'prabandha' gloss is recalled from GST ch. 18 (Uttaratantra); verse not checked.

definitions.definition: Action tantra: the class emphasizing external ritual, purity, offerings and mantra recitation to a deity visualized in front (e.g. Susiddhikara, Subāhuparipṛcchā); first of the Tibetan fourfold classification, recognized in Indian doxographies as well.
Conduct (or performance) tantra: balancing outer ritual and inner yoga (e.g. the Mahāvairocana, Vajrapāṇyabhiṣeka); second of the fourfold classification.

notes: Homonym: 'caryā' also names the siddhas' conduct and their songs (trm:carya).

definitions.definition: Yoga tantra: emphasis on inner yoga of identity with the deity in the five-family maṇḍala (Tattvasaṃgraha, Sarvadurgatipariśodhana); third class.

'Unsurpassed yoga tantra': the Tibetan name (rnal 'byor bla med) for the highest class, comprising the Guhyasamāja, Hevajra, Cakrasaṃvara, Kālacakra and related tantras; Indian sources more often speak of yogottara, yoganiruttara/yoginī and mahāyoga tantras.

cross_language.form: rnal 'byor bla na med pa'i rgyud

notes: The Sanskrit form 'anuttarayoga' is itself a back-translation of the Tibetan; Indian texts use yoganiruttara (low confidence on precise attestations).

definitions.definition: 'Higher yoga' tantras, an Indian class name for the Guhyasamāja group (later Tibetan 'father tantras').

Tantras of the yoginīs (also 'yoganiruttara', 'the unexcelled yoga'): the Cakrasaṃvara, Hevajra, Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa and related cycles, with female deities, cremation-ground imagery and the yoga of bliss (later Tibetan 'mother tantras').
'Great yoga' tantras, an Indian class (Guhyasamāja, Māyājāla) and in the Nyingma nine vehicles the seventh vehicle.
Father tantra: a later Tibetan category for highest-yoga tantras emphasizing means, winds and the illusory body (the Guhyasamāja, Yamāri cycles).

notes: A Tibetan classification, not Indian; labeled accordingly.

definitions.definition: Mother tantra: a later Tibetan category for highest-yoga tantras emphasizing wisdom, bliss and clear light (Cakrasaṃvara, Hevajra).
Non-dual tantra: a Tibetan category for tantras held to balance both (the Kālacakra in some systems, the Hevajra in the Sakya view).

notes: Tibetan classification; assignments differ by school.

definitions.definition: The indestructible: emptiness and gnosis that cannot be split; as a ritual implement held in the right hand it symbolizes means (compassion), joined with the bell of wisdom.
The ritual bell held in the left hand, symbol of wisdom (emptiness), paired with the vajra.

The 'vajra-holder', the form of the Buddha who teaches the tantras and the state of union attained at the end of the path ('the great Vajradhara', Pañcakrama 1.7); the guru is to be seen as inseparable from him.

'Vajra being': the lord of the five families and the purified nature of the practitioner; in the Sekoddeśa the one consecrated with the fourth consecration becomes Vajrasattva, the progenitor of all protectors.
The primordial buddha 'without beginning or end' (Nāmasaṃgīti 100), gnosis as its only eye.
The Kālacakra's name for the non-dual gnosis of immutable bliss and empty form, source of the root tantra ('Paramādibuddha'); not a creator.
The wrathful, cremation-ground form of the buddha — Cakrasaṃvara, Hevajra and others — embodying great bliss; the Hevajra glosses 'he' as compassion and 'vajra' as wisdom.
Female tantric deity or realized woman, 'sky-goer', guardian and source of instructions; the dohās speak of 'the secret speech of the ḍākinīs' and warn that ḍākinīs punish breaches of pledge.
Female practitioner or goddess of the maṇḍala; the Yoginī tantras are 'their' tantras.
Selflessness personified as the goddess Nairātmyā, Hevajra's consort, who appeared to Virūpa; in the dohā commentaries she is the avadhūtī and the innate.
The vajra master who confers consecration and instruction; greater than the Buddha in kindness because he gives the instruction (Pañcakrama 4.2); qualities listed in the Gurupañcāśikā.
The 'true guru' (bla ma dam pa), from whose mouth alone the innate is found (Saraha, Tōh 2292 no. 6; People Dohā v19), who points out mind's nature 'as a finger points at the sky'.
The vajra master, to be examined before the bond and then regarded as inseparable from Vajradhara.
A 'great adept' who has attained the supreme siddhi (mahāmudrā) — especially the eighty-four of Abhayadatta's lives.
One who has attained siddhi; the tantric adept of the lives and songs, often living in a lay trade or as a wandering yogin.
Attainment: the common (mundane) attainments — powers such as flight, the sword, the elixir, invisibility, the eight great siddhis — and the supreme attainment, mahāmudrā / buddhahood.
'Knowledge-holder': a mantra practitioner who has attained a level of siddhi; the vidyādhara vow is the tantric vow.

Consecration (empowerment) by a vajra master that authorizes and ripens the disciple: in the highest tantras four — vase, secret, wisdom-gnosis and the fourth; in the Kālacakra, seven 'child' consecrations and the higher ones, 'three conventional, the fourth ultimate'.
The vase consecration, first of the four; purifies the body and authorizes the generation stage.
The secret consecration, second of the four; purifies speech and authorizes the yoga of the channels and winds (restricted content).
The wisdom-gnosis consecration, third of the four; purifies mind and introduces the joys (restricted content); forbidden to celibates by Atiśa.

cross_language.form: shes rab ye shes kyi dbang

definitions.definition: The fourth consecration, 'ultimate' (Sekoddeśa 8), introducing the innate gnosis; in Tibetan often the 'word consecration'.
The pledge undertaken at consecration — to the guru, the vajra kin, the deity, and the view and conduct; its root breaches are the fourteen downfalls, whose ripening is described as the vajra hell.
Tilopa warns that guarding vows conceptually falls from the meaning of the pledge (Gaṅgāmā v22–23).
Root downfall: one of the fourteen breaches that destroy the tantric pledge.
Gross (secondary) downfall of the tantric vow, listed after the root downfalls in the Advayavajrasaṃgraha.
The 'vajra hell' into which one falls who breaks the tantric pledge or practises without consecration (Queen Dohā v15–17).

Vow (the prātimokṣa, bodhisattva and vidyādhara vows); in the Cakrasaṃvara cycle also 'binding' or 'supreme bliss' — the commentators read Saṃvara as the supreme bliss that binds the wheel of phenomena.

notes: The 'supreme bliss' etymology is the Tibetan translators' (bde mchog).

definitions.definition: The secret: the tantras are to be kept from the unconsecrated; revealing the secret to the unripe is a root downfall.

The sacred circle — palace and assembly of deities (e.g. the Vajradhātu, Womb, Guhyasamāja and Heruka maṇḍalas) into which the disciple is introduced and as which the world and body are seen; also the offering of the universe.
Sacred formula of a deity; the mantra way is named after it; its essence is the vajra recitation of OṂ ĀḤ HŪṂ with the breath (Pañcakrama 1).
Saraha: 'I have not seen a single mantra or tantra' — the innate is beyond mantra (People Dohā v41).
The three syllables of the body, speech and mind vajras of all tathāgatas, recited with the breath in vajra recitation.
Seal: a hand gesture; the four seals of the Tattvasaṃgraha and of Advayavajra (karma-, dharma-, mahā-, samaya-mudrā); also the consort.
The four seals: action seal, dharma seal, great seal and pledge seal, which Advayavajra orders as stages leading from the action seal to the pledge seal.
Saraha criticizes those who 'set out the four seals by distinguishing the moments' and take the experience for the innate (King Dohā v27).
The 'action seal': a physical consort in the yoga of the higher consecrations; summary only (restricted).
The 'gnosis seal': a visualized consort (as distinct from the karmamudrā).
The 'dharma seal': the innate nature, the avadhūtī between lalanā and rasanā, cause of the great seal (Advayavajra).
The 'pledge seal': Vajradhara's radiating as Heruka with the enjoyment and emanation bodies for the sake of beings (Advayavajra).
The 'great seal': the innate nature of mind, realized through the guru's instruction, beyond meditation and non-meditation; 'mind without aim is mahāmudrā' (Gaṅgāmā v17).

The third of the four seals: without own-being, like the clear autumn midday sky, the single nature of existence and nirvāṇa, whose body is objectless compassion and whose form is great bliss (Advayavajra); the supreme siddhi reached by the buddhas (Pañcakrama 5.28).

notes: Homonym: in haṭha yoga mahāmudrā is a seal-practice (see U28/U29 definitions of the same id).

definitions.definition: The 'means of accomplishment': the ritual-meditative text and practice by which the practitioner arises as the deity (the Sādhanamālā collects over three hundred); in the Guhyasamāja one of the four branches (service, near-attainment, attainment, great attainment).

'Service' or 'approach': the first of the four branches of practice; in GST ch. 18 the ordinary service is the fourfold vajra (emptiness, seed, image, syllables) and the supreme service the six-branch yoga.
The tantric fire offering for pacifying, increasing, subjugating and destroying; Saraha mocks it when done without knowledge (People Dohā v2–3).
The tantric feast, a gathering of yogins and yoginīs with offerings, song and dance; summary only.
The cremation ground, the setting of Heruka's maṇḍala and of the yogin's observance ('the unsurpassed cremation ground, great place of awakening', Tōh 2292 no. 61).
Sacred seat: the twenty-four (or more) sites of the Heruka maṇḍala in India, and their inner counterparts in the body; the Hevajra correlates classes of sites with the bodhisattva grounds.
The skull-topped staff carried by herukas and yogins (Queen Dohā v50–51).
The skull-cup of the heruka and yogin; Kapālapa's song calls such ornaments adventitious.
Placing syllables or deities on the body (in GST 18 the 'fourfold vajra' of ordinary service ends with 'placing the syllables').
The generation stage: arising as the deity in the maṇḍala from emptiness through seed syllables, with clarity and divine pride; the basis for the completion stage ('a staircase', Pañcakrama 1.2).

The completion (perfection) stage: the yogas of the channels, winds and drops leading through the empties to clear light, illusory body and union; one with the generation stage in union (Pañcakrama 5.20).
Deity yoga: meditating oneself as the deity, whose form is appearance inseparable from emptiness; 'there is no meditator … mantra and deity abide in the nature free of elaboration' (Hevajra I.5).
The 'pledge being': the deity as visualized by the practitioner, into which the gnosis being is drawn.
The 'gnosis being': the actual deity invited to merge with the visualized one; Mañjuśrī as gnosis-being in the Nāmasaṃgīti.
Manifest awakening: the five manifest awakenings of the Tattvasaṃgraha; in the Pañcakrama the fourth stage (clear light).
Vajra recitation: joining the mantra OṂ ĀḤ HŪṂ with the movement of the winds, the first stage of the Pañcakrama (speech isolation).
Speech isolation: the stage of vajra recitation in the Ārya scheme.
Mind isolation (the Pañcakrama's 'cittanidhyapti'): the stage in which the three appearances and the four empties are experienced.
Body isolation: seeing the aggregates and elements as deities, listed before speech isolation in the six-stage presentation of the Ārya school.
Self-consecration: the illusory body arisen from wind and mind, the third stage of the Pañcakrama, 'the vision of conventional truth', obtained only by the guru's grace.

notes: Homonym: in haṭha/tantric Hindu anatomy svādhiṣṭhāna is the second cakra (other units' definitions).

definitions.definition: The illusory body, of wind and mind, like a reflection or a rainbow; the conventional truth that joins with clear light (Pañcakrama; Tilopa's Ṣaḍdharmopadeśa).
Clear light, the fourth empty (sarvaśūnya), the cause of the world and the ultimate truth of the two (Pañcakrama 2.5, 3.13–15).
The clear light of one's own mind, never obscured by aeons of saṃsāra (Gaṅgāmā v12).
Union: where saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, the two truths, generation and completion, wisdom and compassion become one (Pañcakrama 5); the goal of the path.
The 'all-empty', fourth of the four empties, identical with clear light.
'Light', the first empty and first of the three appearances (light, light-appearance, light-attainment) in the Pañcakrama.
In the Pañcakrama the thirty-three, forty and seven 'natures' — conceptual states associated with the three appearances (80 in all), which run by the movement of the winds.

notes: Homonym of Sāṃkhya prakṛti; this is the Ārya-school technical sense.

definitions.definition: Channel of the subtle body: thirty-two (Hevajra) or 72,000, of which three are principal — lalanā, rasanā and avadhūtī.
The central channel, 'free of the duality of grasped and grasper'; above the navel also called suṣumṇā (Sekoddeśa 50); into it the winds are drawn in the completion stage.

equivalents.note: The Sekoddeśa names the avadhūtī above the navel suṣumṇā; the Hindu haṭha suṣumṇā is the corresponding central channel in a different system.

definitions.definition: The left channel (moon, wisdom); the Sekoddeśa equates it with iḍā.
The right channel (sun, means); the Sekoddeśa equates it with piṅgalā.
Wheel of channels: in the Hevajra four — emanation (navel), dharma (heart), enjoyment (throat), great bliss (head); in the Kālacakra six.
Wind, 'the vehicle of consciousness', fivefold and tenfold (Pañcakrama 1.3); its dissolution in the central channel brings the empties and clear light.
Saraha: 'where wind and mind do not move, there take rest' (People Dohā v26–27).
The 'drop': the essential drops of the subtle body (white and red), the moon at the crown; also the drop visualized at the nose tip (Ajogi) and the 'great drop' among the ten signs.

The mind of awakening: conventional (the aspiration) and ultimate (emptiness and compassion inseparable, 'free of all entities … one's own mind unborn', GST 2); in the completion stage also the white drop.
Inner heat, 'the fierce woman' who blazes at the navel and melts the moon at the head (Hevajra I.1); one of Tilopa's six dharmas; restricted practice.

equivalents.note: Both are a feminine inner power at the base/navel rising through the central channel; the systems and goals differ (Buddhist: melting bliss joined with emptiness).

definitions.definition: The four joys of the completion stage and consecration — joy, supreme joy, joy of cessation, innate joy.
The innate joy, the fourth; Saraha: 'at the time of the fourth joy the natural state is known in experience' (People Dohā v116).

cross_language.form: lhan cig skyes pa'i dga' ba

definitions.definition: The innate (co-emergent): the nature of mind, neither thing nor no-thing, found only through the true guru and realized as the one taste of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa (Saraha; Tōh 2292).
The innate joy and gnosis introduced in the fourth consecration; 'not told by another nor found anywhere, known by oneself through merit and service to the guru' (Hevajra I.8).
Great bliss: the bliss joined with emptiness that is the nature of the innate and of the goal; the fourth cakra at the head is 'of great bliss'.
Great passion: passion purified as great bliss and compassion; 'great, great, great passion' is a name of Mañjuśrī (Nāmasaṃgīti 30); non-abiding nirvāṇa is great passion (Sekoddeśa 82).
Saraha: turn the three realms into the one colour of great passion (People Dohā v28).
The natural, 'native' state (Tibetan gnyug ma) that the siddhas point to — uncontrived mind.

notes: Sanskrit form reconstructed from the Tibetan gnyug ma; the Apabhraṃśa dohās use ṇia/nia (low).

definitions.definition: 'Mind itself' (sems nyid): the nature of mind, 'the seed of everything, from which saṃsāra and nirvāṇa radiate' (People Dohā v42–43).
Self-awareness (rang rig): 'Kye ho, this is self-awareness' (People Dohā v33); the realization known by oneself.

notes: Also a Yogācāra/pramāṇa term (reflexive awareness) — see U41.

definitions.definition: Non-mentation, 'not engaging the mind' (yid la mi byed pa): Maitrīpa's key term for mahāmudrā, glossed as the union of clear light (a) and self-consecration (manasikāra), not mere blankness; Tilopa's 'not engaging the mind, free of all intent'.
One taste (ro gcig): the realization that all dharmas are of one taste in the innate (Queen Dohā v10; Tōh 2292 no. 20).
Equal taste (ro mnyam): the non-difference of all tastes, of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, for the realized (Tōh 2292 nos. 29, 66, 75).
'Ordinary knowing' that awakens in the centre of the heart (Koṭali's song, Tōh 2292 no. 44); a key Kagyu term for the nature of mind.
Intentional (or 'twilight') language: coded speech of the tantras and songs whose outer sense hides an inner yogic meaning; the Hevajra (II.3) gives a lexicon of it.

notes: The reading sandhā- vs sandhyā- is debated; both occur.

definitions.definition: A rhymed couplet in Apabhraṃśa; the siddhas' teaching songs are 'treasuries of dohās' (dohākoṣa).
(1) The yogin's conduct or observance (spyod pa), undertaken after realization; (2) the caryā songs (caryāgīti) sung to rāgas at the feast.
The 'observance' of the realized yogin — wandering, the cremation ground, the 'mad' conduct — to test and deepen realization; only after realization (Mekopa; Nāgārjuna's song).
The 'mad observance' (smyon pa'i brtul zhugs), acting as a madman in the world after realizing equality.
The dharma body: 'liberation in an instant is called dharmakāya' (Queen Dohā v8); appearances and sounds are primordially dharmakāya (Tōh 2292 no. 30).
The enjoyment body; with the emanation body one of the two form bodies that arise through aspiration and compassion (Queen Dohā v64–68).
The emanation body, appearing variously to those to be trained.
The 'essence body', the fourth body, the inseparability of the others; its bliss is 'the great enjoyment' (Queen Dohā v65).
The body of great bliss, a fourth (or fifth) body in the Kālacakra and Hevajra systems, correlated with the fourth consecration.

The five buddha families — tathāgata (Vairocana), vajra (Akṣobhya), jewel (Ratnasambhava), lotus (Amitābha) and action (Amoghasiddhi) — into which the aggregates, elements, afflictions and gnoses are sorted.
The five gnoses — mirror-like, equality, discriminating, accomplishing and dharmadhātu gnosis — the purified five aggregates/afflictions, each belonging to a family.
One of the five gnoses: mirror-like gnosis (purified form / hatred), vajra family; the correlations of aggregate and affliction vary between systems.

cross_language.form: me long lta bu'i ye shes

notes: The pairings of gnosis, aggregate, affliction and family follow one common scheme; others exist.

definitions.definition: One of the five gnoses: gnosis of equality (purified feeling / pride), jewel family; the correlations of aggregate and affliction vary between systems.

cross_language.form: mnyam pa nyid kyi ye shes

notes: The pairings of gnosis, aggregate, affliction and family follow one common scheme; others exist.

definitions.definition: One of the five gnoses: discriminating gnosis (purified perception / desire), lotus family; the correlations of aggregate and affliction vary between systems.

notes: The pairings of gnosis, aggregate, affliction and family follow one common scheme; others exist.

definitions.definition: One of the five gnoses: accomplishing gnosis (purified formations / envy), action family; the correlations of aggregate and affliction vary between systems.

cross_language.form: bya ba grub pa'i ye shes

notes: The pairings of gnosis, aggregate, affliction and family follow one common scheme; others exist.

definitions.definition: One of the five gnoses: gnosis of the dharma-sphere (purified consciousness / delusion), tathāgata family; the correlations of aggregate and affliction vary between systems.

cross_language.form: chos kyi dbyings kyi ye shes

notes: The pairings of gnosis, aggregate, affliction and family follow one common scheme; others exist.

definitions.definition: The three vajras — body, speech and mind — of all tathāgatas (the Guhyasamāja's opening), with the syllables OṂ ĀḤ HŪṂ.

cross_language.form: rdo rje gsum / sku gsung thugs

definitions.definition: The 'wheel of time': name of the tantra and deity; time (kāla) is means/bliss, the wheel (cakra) wisdom/empty form; the outer, inner and other wheels.
Empty form: the image arisen from emptiness seen in the six-branch yoga after the ten signs; the cause sealed by immutable bliss (Sekoddeśa 146).
Immutable (imperishable) bliss, the result that seals empty form; the unchanging bliss that does not fall away.
The imperishable: the unchanging bliss and gnosis of the Kālacakra ('the supreme imperishable', Sekoddeśa 77).
The letter/syllable: 'A, foremost of letters, the supreme imperishable' (Nāmasaṃgīti 28).
The six-branch yoga — withdrawal, meditation, breath control, retention, recollection, absorption — the supreme service in GST ch. 18 and the completion stage of the Kālacakra.
Recollection, the fifth branch of the six-branch yoga: recollecting the form visualized, when an appearance arises (GST 18.150).
Withdrawal, first branch of the six-branch yoga: the ten senses each abiding in its own place (GST 18.139).
Retention, fourth branch of the six-branch yoga: one's mantra in the heart placed in the drop of life-wind (GST 18.145).
Third branch of the six-branch yoga in the Buddhist order (after dhyāna): the breath of the five gnoses imagined as a five-coloured jewel at the nose tip (GST 18.144; Pañcakrama 1.10–15).
The hidden kingdom in the north from which the Kālacakra came, ruled by the dharma-kings and the kalkins; its future kalkin will defeat the barbarians.
Title of the kings of Śambhala from Mañjuśrīyaśas, who united the castes into one vajra family.

The letter A, 'foremost of all letters, the supreme imperishable, unborn' (Nāmasaṃgīti 28–29), the door of all dharmas because they are originally unborn (Mahāvairocana; Hevajra as quoted by Advayavajra).
The two syllables E and VAṂ, 'thus', read as wisdom and means, the lotus and the vajra, the union with which the sūtras begin.
Seed syllable from which the deity arises in the generation stage; the seed syllables of the five families in dream yoga (Ṣaḍdharmopadeśa).
The intermediate state between death and rebirth, in which the yogin practises deity yoga or rests in reality to block rebirth (Tilopa, from Sukhasiddhi).
Transference of consciousness at death ('pho ba), sixth of Tilopa's dharmas; restricted.

notes: Sanskrit equivalents of 'pho ba vary in the sources (low certainty).

definitions.definition: Entering another's body (grong 'jug), taught with transference in Tilopa's Ṣaḍdharmopadeśa.

The dohās speak of abiding on 'the fourteenth ground' (People Dohā v110; Queen Dohā v81); the Hevajra correlates the sacred sites with the ten grounds; later systems count thirteen or more tantric grounds.
The form bodies (enjoyment and emanation), arising through aspiration and compassion (Queen Dohā v67).
Non-dual gnosis: union, non-abiding nirvāṇa, buddhahood; words like 'unborn' point only to it (Pañcakrama 5.25–27).

cross_language.form: gnyis su med pa'i ye shes

definitions.definition: Non-abiding nirvāṇa: identical with non-dual gnosis (Pañcakrama 5.25) and with 'great passion' (Sekoddeśa 82).

cross_language.form: mi gnas pa'i mya ngan las 'das pa

definitions.definition: Emptiness, which without compassion is not the supreme path (People Dohā v15–17).
Compassion, which alone keeps one in saṃsāra; joined with emptiness it is the path (People Dohā v15–17); its flower and fruit are benefit for others.
Wisdom (emptiness), the feminine pole (bell, lotus, lalanā, the consort) joined with means.
Means (compassion, great bliss), the masculine pole (vajra, rasanā) joined with wisdom; 'by the very deeds that bind, joined with means, beings are freed' (Cittaviśuddhiprakaraṇa 6).
